category_title: Aboriginal adolescents in alternative education who resist traditional pedagogy but engage with digital multiliteracies
minimal_context: The student is in a grade 7-8 alternative education classroom being assigned a project to interview a family member about residential schools.
dialogue:
TUTOR: For our next project, I want each of you to interview one of your family members about their experiences in residential schools.

STUDENT: I'm not doing that. That topic is boring.

TUTOR: This is the assignment we are doing today. Please start writing down your interview questions.

STUDENT: I don't care. Whenever you give us work to do on our own like this, I'm not doing it. I'll just walk out of the classroom.

TUTOR: You need to stay in the classroom and complete the assigned interview project.

STUDENT: I refuse. We want to investigate gangs, weapons, and drugs to create a video that we'll call 'Do the Right Thing'.

options.A: Ask the student, "Why? Why do you think that?" to prompt justification for their refusal and their interest in the alternative video topic.
options.B: Create a simple walk-through guide for the interview project that the student can access independently whenever they need to troubleshoot the assignment.
options.C: Use gradual proximity by sitting near the student without forcing talk, using quiet speech, and eventually introducing gentle physical contact during the session.
options.D: Be extremely flexible with the project plans, accept the student's lived experiences, and invite them to use their funds of knowledge in multiliteracies.
